source.title: Strength and Power Training in Rehabilitation: Underpinning Principles and Practical Strategies to Return Athletes to High Performance

paper.citation: Maestroni L., Read P., Bishop C., Turner A. Strength and Power Training in Rehabilitation: Underpinning Principles and Practical Strategies to Return Athletes to High Performance. Sports Medicine. 2020;50(2):239-252. doi:10.1007/s40279-019-01195-6.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Which residual neuromuscular deficits commonly remain after musculoskeletal injury, and which strength and power strategies can be used to address them during rehabilitation? Participants: No single cohort; the article reviews evidence from athletic and rehabilitation populations. Sport and level: Athletic populations across sports. Design: Narrative evidence review with practical programming examples. Exposure or intervention: Maximal-strength, ballistic-power, rate-of-force-development, and reactive-strength training.
paper.tldr: Residual deficits in maximal strength, rate of force development, and reactive strength are documented after musculoskeletal injury. Rehabilitation should prepare athletes for loads and velocities across the force-velocity spectrum rather than restoring high force at low velocity alone. Build late rehabilitation as physical preparation, not merely symptom resolution.
paper.methods: Design: Narrative evidence review with practical programming examples. Exposure or intervention: Maximal-strength, ballistic-power, rate-of-force-development, and reactive-strength training. Comparator: Varies across the cited literature. Measurements and outcomes: Strength, power, rate of force development, reactive strength, sprinting, and jumping. Analysis: Applied synthesis of mechanisms, documented deficits, and training strategies.
paper.findings: Residual deficits in maximal strength, rate of force development, and reactive strength are documented after musculoskeletal injury. Rehabilitation should prepare athletes for loads and velocities across the force-velocity spectrum rather than restoring high force at low velocity alone. The review cites evidence suggesting maximal-strength training should remain dominant in relatively weak athletes below approximately 1.6 times body mass in the back squat, while stressing the broader individual context.
paper.limitations: The paper integrates heterogeneous injuries and supporting studies, so its programming examples are principles rather than validated universal return-to-play criteria. Interpretation: Strength ratios and loading benchmarks must be adjusted for the athlete, injury, exercise technique, sport demands, and stage of tissue recovery.
paper.practicalImplications: Build late rehabilitation as physical preparation, not merely symptom resolution. Profile which qualities remain constrained, select exercises by the force and velocity demands they expose, and progress from force capacity toward fast and reactive expression. Treat any strength benchmark as context for programming, not as a stand-alone clearance threshold.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete development, build late rehabilitation as physical preparation, not merely symptom resolution. Profile which qualities remain constrained, select exercises by the force and velocity demands they expose, and progress from force capacity toward fast and reactive expression. Treat any strength benchmark as context for programming, not as a stand-alone clearance threshold. Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, build late rehabilitation as physical preparation, not merely symptom resolution. Profile which qualities remain constrained, select exercises by the force and velocity demands they expose, and progress from force capacity toward fast and reactive expression. Treat any strength benchmark as context for programming, not as a stand-alone clearance threshold. Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.
